sentences.text: Cartorhynchus was a small animal measuring about 40 cm in length, possessing a lizard-like body and a short torso.
It is characterized by a short, constricted snout and multiple rows of molar-like teeth growing on the inner surface of its jaw bones.
The animal had limbs with extensive cartilage that could bend like flippers, possibly allowing it to walk on land.
Extensive cartilage at the wrist joint likely allowed these flippers to bend without an elbow, similar to juvenile sea turtles.
The fossil was discovered in 2011 by Ryosuke Motani and Da-yong Jiang in a mine at Majiashan, Anhui, China.
Ryosuke Motani and colleagues described the specimen as a new genus and species, Cartorhynchus lenticarpus, in Nature in 2014.
The specimen was assigned the field number MT-II and the specimen number AGB 6257 at the Anhui Geological Museum.
Because the specimen was too fragile to open, researchers used micro-CT scanning performed at the Yinghua Testing Company in Shanghai to examine the interior of the jaws.
Cartorhynchus possessed molariform teeth, indicating a diet that included hard-shelled animals.
Researchers suggest Cartorhynchus preyed on hard-shelled invertebrates using suction feeding, though the exact mechanism of its inward-directed teeth remains unknown.
Researchers suggested Cartorhynchus had an amphibious lifestyle aided by a short trunk, snout, and thickened ribs acting as ballast.
Cartorhynchus belongs to the clade Nasorostra, which is the sister group to Ichthyopterygia.
In 2014, researchers named the group containing Cartorhynchus and Ichthyopterygia Ichthyosauriformes, and the larger group including Hupehsuchia Ichthyosauromorpha.
The animal was part of a rapid diversification of marine reptiles during the Spathian substage, occurring about one million years after the Permian-Triassic extinction event.
Cartorhynchus lived during the Early Triassic epoch, approximately 248 million years ago, at the beginning of the Lower Triassic (Olenekian stage).
It lived in an oceanic basin located relatively far from the coast during the Middle Triassic.

Researchers hypothesized in 2014 that Cartorhynchus was a suction feeder, but a 2020 study concluded it was a durophagous feeder based on its molariform teeth, suggesting it was likely restricted to feeding on small prey.
Researchers suggest that the inability of the lower jaw bones to fuse tightly in Cartorhynchus was a characteristic shared with toothless hupehsuchians.
